name: Ch’ēn Tzŭ-ang
bio: Ch’ēn Tzŭ-ang (AD 656–698) was famous for impromptu descriptive verse of the kind the Chinese call “Ying.” His passionate disposition brought him into trouble with the magistrate of his district, who had him cast into prison, where he died at the age of forty-two.
The poems here are Arthur Waley’s version in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918); L. Cranmer-Byng’s version in A Lute of Jade (1909), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poems.title: Business Men
poems.author: Ch’ēn Tzŭ-ang
poems.collection: A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918)
poems.text:
Business men boast of their skill and cunning
But in philosophy they are like little children.
Bragging to each other of successful depredations
They neglect to consider the ultimate fate of the body.
What should they know of the Master of Dark Truth
Who saw the wide world in a jade cup,
By illumined conception got clear of Heaven and Earth:
On the chariot of Mutation entered the Gate of Immutability?

poems.title: The Last Revel
poems.author: Ch’ēn Tzŭ-ang
poems.text:
From silver lamps a thin blue smoke is streaming,
And golden vases ’mid the feast are gleaming;
Now sound the lutes in unison,
Within the gates our lives are one.
We’ll think not of the parting ways
As long as dawn delays.

When in tall trees the dying moonbeams quiver:
When floods of fire efface the Silver River,
Then comes the hour when I must seek
Lo-Yang beyond the furthest peak.
But the warm twilight round us twain
Will never rise again.

poems.title: Regrets
poems.author: Ch’ēn Tzŭ-ang
poems.text:
My eyes saw not the men of old;
And now their age away has rolled
I weep — to think I shall not see
The heroes of posterity!

poems.title: Against Idols
poems.author: Ch’ēn Tzŭ-ang
poems.text:
On Self the Prophet never rests his eye,
His to relieve the doom of humankind;
No fairy palaces beyond the sky,
Rewards to come, are present to his mind.

And I have heard the faith by Buddha taught
Lauded as pure and free from earthly taint;
Why then these carved and graven idols, fraught
With gold and silver, gems, and jade, and paint?

The heavens that roof this earth, mountain and dale,
All that is great and grand shall pass away;
And if the art of gods may not prevail.
Shall man's poor handiwork escape decay?

Fools that ye are! In this ignoble light
The true faith fades and passes out of sight.

poems.title: On a Gate-Tower at Yu-chou
poems.author: Ch’ēn Tzŭ-ang
poems.translator: trans. Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu (1929)
poems.text:
Where, before me, are the ages that have gone?
And where, behind me, are the coming generations?
I think of heaven and earth, without limit, without end,
And I am all alone and my tears fall down.

poems.title: 贈喬侍郎 (Zeng qiao shi lang)
poems.author: Ch’ēn Tzŭ-ang
poems.collection: 千家詩 (Poems of a Thousand Poets)
poems.text:
漢廷榮巧宦，雲閣薄邊功。
可憐驄馬使，白首爲誰雄。

poems.title: 春夜別友人 (Chun ye bie you ren)
poems.author: Ch’ēn Tzŭ-ang
poems.collection: 千家詩 (Poems of a Thousand Poets)
poems.text:
銀燭吐青煙，金尊對綺筵。
離堂思琴瑟，別路繞山川。
明月懸高樹，長河沒曉天。
悠悠洛陽道，此會在何年。

poems.title: 送著作佐郎崔融等從樑王東征 (Song zhu zuo zuo lang cui rong deng cong liang wang dong zheng)
poems.author: Ch’ēn Tzŭ-ang
poems.collection: 千家詩 (Poems of a Thousand Poets)
poems.text:
金天方肅殺，白露始專征。
王師非樂戰，之子慎佳兵。
海氣侵南部，邊風掃北平。
莫賣盧龍塞，歸邀麟閣名。

poems.title: 登幽州臺歌 (Deng you zhou tai ge)
poems.author: Ch’ēn Tzŭ-ang
poems.collection: 唐詩三百首 (Three Hundred Tang Poems)
poems.text:
前不見古人，後不見來者。
念天地之悠悠，獨愴然而涕下。
